science_records.claim: For a one-dimensional motion, displacement is final position minus initial position and distance is total path length.
science_records.law_or_model: signed one-dimensional position and cumulative distance
assumptions: One fixed coordinate axis is declared
A common reference frame for all positions
conditions_and_limits: The absolute value of net displacement never exceeds path length.
A coordinate reversal changes displacement sign but does not alter path distance.
science_records.units_and_signs: x and Δx in m, east positive unless specified; distance is nonnegative.

science_records.claim: For two bodies' velocities measured in the same non-rotating reference frame, relative velocity along one axis is the signed difference.
science_records.law_or_model: v(B/A) = vB − vA; Galilean composition in classical one-dimensional kinematics
assumptions: The compared velocities are signed on the same axis
Speeds sufficiently slow that elementary Galilean composition applies
The frame is suitably inertial for subsequent Newtonian force reasoning
conditions_and_limits: Relative velocities stated in different intermediate frames must be composed in order.
Do not add unsigned speeds automatically or infer meeting time without initial separation.
science_records.units_and_signs: Signed velocities in m/s, signed east positive.

science_records.claim: On a velocity-time graph, the signed area over a time interval is displacement, whereas total distance sums the magnitudes of segment contributions.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise v–t area and x–t slope
assumptions: The graphed quantities use a fixed coordinate system
Time interval is partitioned at genuine changes of velocity law
conditions_and_limits: Signed area is not automatically positive distance.
Vertical velocity jumps are idealizations; actual finite force implies finite-time change.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; time s; signed area m; positive and negative velocities are directions.

science_records.claim: Each position formula applies only over the interval whose motion conditions define it.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise constant-velocity motion and interval-filtered intersections
assumptions: Correct start times and initial positions are known
Each interval's velocity law is valid only within declared bounds
conditions_and_limits: A solution outside its interval is inadmissible even if the algebra is correct.
After a stop, reversal or delayed departure, use a new position expression with continuity at the boundary.
science_records.units_and_signs: Global clock t in s; positions m; each segment retains signed velocity m/s.

science_records.claim: Over a time interval, average speed is total path length divided by duration; average signed velocity is net displacement divided by duration.
science_records.law_or_model: averages from path length and signed position
assumptions: One global start and end time
Correct distinction between path length and signed position
conditions_and_limits: Replacing displacement with path length in average velocity is invalid.
An object may have zero average velocity while having nonzero average speed.
science_records.units_and_signs: Speed ≥0, velocity has sign, both measured in m/s; length in metres and duration in seconds.

science_records.claim: For motion split into constant-velocity intervals, total distance is the sum of |v_i| Δt_i and net displacement is the sum of v_i Δt_i.
assumptions: Each stage's signed velocity and interval duration are defined
Each interval is counted once and no time gap is overlooked
conditions_and_limits: The magnitude of net displacement never exceeds total distance.
A reversal makes the algebraic displacement sum differ from summed distance.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; time s; sums produce metres.

science_records.claim: For a straight-line segment on an x–t graph, signed slope Δx/Δt equals the constant velocity in that interval.
science_records.law_or_model: position-time slope and inverse graphical reconstruction
assumptions: Position and time axes have known scale and units
Motion is piecewise constant velocity for straight graph segments
conditions_and_limits: A horizontal x–t segment means rest in that frame, not zero position.
Graph height on x–t is position, whereas graph height on v–t is velocity.
science_records.units_and_signs: Position in m; time s; slope m/s.

core1a.phenomenon: A commuter can end near the starting point after a long journey: the speedometer and displacement tell different stories.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A description of motion begins with position, not the answer to a numerical formula. Mark the commuter's origin and east-positive coordinate. Each trip leg changes the position by a signed amount, but each contributes a positive path length. Average speed is the accumulated path length divided by elapsed time; average velocity is the single net position change divided by the same time. The two averages can differ even for a perfectly continuous trip, and average velocity becomes zero on a round trip. Reversing the coordinate direction reverses the velocity component without changing any physical speed. Build both numerical sums from the travel log before deciding which one the experiment measures. A graph of position versus time makes the change in direction visible, while a ledger of distances preserves how far the person actually travelled.
prerequisites: PH01-M01 reference frame and positive direction

derivation_steps.action: Mark every leg with its signed displacement and duration.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Displacement is the difference between endpoint positions, and its sign depends on the chosen axis.

derivation_steps.action: Sum signed legs for Δx, and absolute leg lengths for path distance.
derivation_steps.why_valid: A reversal cancels some signed displacement but never cancels distance already travelled.

derivation_steps.action: Divide the appropriate numerator by the same total elapsed time.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The definition of each average requires the corresponding path or net position quantity.

model_limits: Interval averages do not determine detailed instantaneous velocity.
Different direction conventions change signed velocity, not path length.
A single scalar speed does not carry the direction needed for a meeting equation.

progressive_examples.problem: A pupil walks 18 m east and 7 m west in 5 s. Compare distance and displacement.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Distance 18+7=25 m, signed displacement 18−7=+11 m, average speed 5 m/s, average velocity +2.2 m/s.

progressive_examples.problem: A runner travels east 40 m in 8 s then west 40 m in 12 s. What does a motion tracker report?
progressive_examples.reasoning: Distance is 80 m and displacement is 0; average speed is 4 m/s and average velocity is zero.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Returning to origin confirms Δx=0 despite movement.

progressive_examples.problem: A cyclist's outward and return legs together total 54 m, with final position +6 m relative to origin. Recover east/west leg lengths.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Write E+W=54 and E−W=6. Solving gives E=30 m and W=24 m. This reconstructs route lengths, not merely an average.

figures.reasoning_step: Keep signed displacement and total travelled distance separate
figures.scene_description: Use the chapter's east-positive out-and-back number-line diagram, with each stage arrow and end marker.

misconception.wrong_model: Average velocity equals average speed whenever elapsed time is the same.
misconception.diagnostic: Ask for both averages on an equal-distance out-and-back walk.
misconception.repair: Use net signed displacement as the numerator of average velocity, and total travelled distance for average speed.

exit_check.task: Travel +12 m in 4 s then −5 m in 1 s. Give both averages and direction.
exit_check.answer: Total distance 17 m; net displacement +7 m; average speed 3.4 m/s; average velocity +1.4 m/s.
exit_check.reasoning: The westward segment is negative in the signed sum but positive in the distance sum.

core1a.phenomenon: A vehicle's recorded position can pause, rise or fall while time keeps increasing; the slopes tell its signed motion.
core1a.scientific_narrative: To read a motion graph, first name both axes. The height of an x–t graph is position, not speed. A horizontal x–t segment means that position is temporarily unchanged, whereas an upward slope means positive signed velocity and a downward slope means negative signed velocity. To obtain a velocity–time graph from a piecewise linear position record, compute the slope for every valid interval and place that signed velocity on the corresponding time segment. Conversely, the signed area under a velocity–time curve reconstructs each position increment, so the endpoint is independently checkable. For distance, however, the magnitudes of areas are added. Crossing the horizontal position axis does not necessarily mean the vehicle has stopped; the slope at that crossing decides velocity. Changing the coordinate origin shifts the whole x–t graph vertically without changing any velocity–time segment. This is a core representation-invariance check.
prerequisites: PH01-M01 graph axes and scaled measurements
PH01-M03 distinction between distance and displacement

derivation_steps.action: Identify whether y-axis reports position or signed velocity.
derivation_steps.why_valid: A height on x–t measures position, but a height on v–t measures velocity; the mathematical action depends on the axis.

derivation_steps.action: Use Δx/Δt to obtain interval velocity; preserve sign and duration.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The slope of each straight position segment equals the constant velocity in that interval.

derivation_steps.action: Reconstruct total displacement from signed v×Δt areas and then independently calculate distance.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Signed areas add to endpoint displacement, while actual travelled distance sums absolute interval lengths.

model_limits: A graph's shape in paper coordinates is not the physical trajectory in space.
A position-axis crossing says nothing by itself about velocity direction.
A sharp velocity jump on an idealized step graph is not a real finite-acceleration process.
For smoothly changing velocity, use the actual area rather than constant-velocity rectangles.

progressive_examples.problem: A cart's position rises from +1 m to +9 m over 4 s as a straight x–t line. Find velocity.
A graph has x=3 at t=0, x=9 at t=3, and x=9 at t=5; reconstruct velocities.
progressive_examples.reasoning: First slope +2 m/s during 0–3; second slope 0 during 3–5. The second interval is stationary at position +9 m.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Signed areas +6 and 0 recover Δx=+6 m.

progressive_examples.problem: An object has velocity +4 m/s for 2 s, then −2 m/s for 5 s. Construct its x–t endpoint from x0=+3 m.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Displacement is 8−10=−2 m, final position x=+1 m. The x–t graph first increases, then decreases past its starting height.
progressive_examples.independent_check: The signed area −2 m matches x_final−x_initial=−2; distance is 18 m.

figures.reasoning_step: Distinguish signed velocity-area from absolute distance
figures.scene_description: Use the chapter's accessible two-interval velocity-time SVG with positive and negative area shading.

misconception.wrong_model: A downward line on a velocity–time graph means the object is going down a hill.
misconception.diagnostic: Compare the velocity graph and its axis labels to a position–time sketch of the same object.
misconception.repair: Read the plotted quantity and its units before interpreting the slope or signed area.

exit_check.task: For v=+2 m/s during 4 s, then −3 m/s during 2 s, calculate net displacement and path distance.
exit_check.answer: Net displacement +8−6=+2 m; path distance 8+6=14 m.
exit_check.reasoning: Signed area of the second segment is negative, but travelled distance remains positive.

core1a.phenomenon: Two moving observers can assign different velocities to the same object, while a mathematical encounter time may fail because the motion model changes.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A position has meaning only relative to a frame and an axis. A journey also has a temporal structure: the physical model for a moving segment cannot be applied after a stop or reversal. Work progressively from signed positions to velocity and acceleration, convert graphs into physical displacement using signed areas, then check the domain of each equation when constructing multi-stage meetings. The reading-first textbook presents each component with a figure, derivation, model limitation and worked check; the advanced inference is rejecting an algebraically valid but physically inadmissible interval and rebuilding the correct motion model.

derivation_steps.action: Declare observer, object, axis and global time before assigning signs.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Relative position and velocity are only well-defined after fixing the measurement frame and coordinate direction.

derivation_steps.action: Translate each position segment into a signed velocity (slope) and verify by graph area.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Velocity is the rate of position change; integrating a constant signed velocity across a segment gives that segment's displacement.

derivation_steps.action: Derive the encounter time within the first valid interval and test it against the interval bounds.
derivation_steps.why_valid: An equation inherits the domain of the motion conditions from which it was constructed; an out-of-domain root is inadmissible.

derivation_steps.action: Construct the second interval's position law continuously from its boundary and re-solve the encounter.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The object's position does not jump merely because it changes speed or direction at the transition.

model_limits: Elementary constant-velocity segment equations are not correct over an interval of continuously changing velocity.
A graph's signed area gives displacement, not necessarily total distance.
Relative velocity subtraction requires consistent frames and sign conventions.
A valid equation root still requires the event to fall within that equation's physical interval.

progressive_examples.problem: A traveller walks 80 m east, then 30 m west in 20 s. Find displacement and distance.
progressive_examples.reasoning: With east positive, displacement is +80−30=+50 m; distance is 80+30=110 m. Average velocity is +2.5 m/s and average speed 5.5 m/s.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Distance ≥ magnitude of displacement; units and signed direction are consistent.

progressive_examples.problem: For 4 s a car has v=+3 m/s, then for 3 s v=−1 m/s. Determine graph area and total path length.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Signed area gives +12−3=+9 m displacement; total distance is 12+3=15 m.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Signed displacement is smaller in magnitude than distance and matches the change in endpoint position.

progressive_examples.problem: A moves east from x=0 at 4 m/s for 4 s then stops; B starts x=40 m and moves west at 3 m/s. When do they meet?
progressive_examples.reasoning: For 0≤t≤4, 4t=40−3t yields t=40/7≈5.71 s, outside its validity. After 4 s A is at x=16, so 16=40−3t gives t=8 s and position x=16 m.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Both actual position models give x=16 at t=8; the first-stage root is rejected as out-of-domain.

figures.reasoning_step: Distinguish path distance and signed displacement
figures.scene_description: Walk from x0 to x80 and back to x50 on east-positive axis, as drawn in textbook PH01 section 1.

figures.reasoning_step: Interpret signed area below velocity-time axis
figures.scene_description: Velocity +3 m/s for 4 s then −1 m/s for 3 s, with signed area colored by sign, as drawn in section 5.

misconception.wrong_model: Treat an algebraic meeting time as valid even when its first-stage motion assumption has ended.
misconception.diagnostic: If equation xA=4t is valid only for t≤4 s, is the solution t=5.71 s a real first-stage meeting?
misconception.repair: Reject the out-of-domain candidate, construct xA=16 for t≥4, then recompute and verify both positions.

exit_check.task: An object moves +3 m/s for 2 s then −1 m/s for 4 s. Compare displacement and distance and explain signs.
exit_check.reasoning: Velocity-time signed areas add for displacement; absolute lengths add for distance.

stages.predict: The position record of a vehicle has a flat interval. Predict whether using its overall average speed as its velocity can find a future meeting.
stages.attempt: A cart has recorded ground positions x=0 m at t=0, x=8 m at t=2 s and x=8 m at t=5 s. After t=5 it moves west at 2 m/s. Another cart is at x=25 m at t=0 and moves west at 1 m/s. Choose and justify the model for their possible meeting, distinguishing average speed, piecewise x–t slopes and relative velocity. Decide whether they meet after t=5.
stages.reconstruct: The first cart moves +4 m/s until t2, rests from t2 to t5, then moves −2 m/s. Its prior average speed over first 5 s is 8/5=1.6 m/s, not its post-t5 velocity. For t≥5, xA=8−2(t−5)=18−2t, xB=25−t. Equality gives t=−7 s, which is outside t≥5; physically, at t5 B is at 20 m, ahead to the east, while A is at 8 m and moving west faster, so the separation increases. No future meeting under the stated model.
stages.diagnose: Separate choosing one averaged velocity for the whole journey from a sign/arithmetical error in the piecewise equation.
stages.repair: Describe each interval from the x–t record, choose correct post-t5 position laws and check candidate time and relative direction.
stages.boundary_test: If after t5 the first cart moves east at +3 m/s instead, is a future meeting possible? Construct and verify the interval root.

Construct the cart's signed ground-frame velocity steps, then its velocities relative to O. Calculate ground-frame net displacement and total path distance; check the translation by signed areas.

stages.predict: If a cart is stationary on the ground but the observer travels east, what sign does the observer measure for cart velocity?
stages.attempt: A cart's ground positions are x=0 at t=0, x=6 at t=2, x=6 at t=5 and x=−3 at t=8 seconds. Observer O moves east at +2 m/s throughout. Construct the cart's signed ground-frame velocity steps, then its velocities relative to O. Calculate ground-frame net displacement and total path distance; check the translation by signed areas.
stages.reconstruct: Ground-frame velocities are +3 m/s for 0–2 s, 0 for 2–5 s, and −3 for 5–8 s. Subtract +2 m/s for observer-relative velocities: +1, −2, −5 m/s. Ground-frame signed areas give +6+0−9=−3 m, the final minus initial position. Total ground distance=6+0+9=15 m. Relative area gives 2−6−15=−19 m, which equals the ground displacement −3 minus observer displacement +16.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether the learner confused x–t graph heights with velocities, added the observer speed instead of subtracting, or used signed area as distance.
stages.repair: For every interval calculate x–t slope; subtract observer velocity using the same sign axis and back-check each displacement.
stages.boundary_test: If O travels west at −2 m/s instead, predict the three observer-relative velocities and explain which ground quantities remain unchanged.

core1b.fresh_task: Cyclist A starts at x=0 and travels east at +4 m/s for 3 seconds, then reverses to −1 m/s. Cyclist B starts at x=30 m and travels west at −4 m/s continuously. Determine their first actual encounter time and position. At that time calculate A's total distance and displacement; justify why a naïve first-stage root is invalid.

stages.predict: Two cyclists' first-stage position equations meet at t=3.75 s but the first cyclist reverses at t=3. Predict whether that is a valid first-stage encounter.
stages.attempt: Cyclist A starts at x=0 and travels east at +4 m/s for 3 seconds, then reverses to −1 m/s. Cyclist B starts at x=30 m and travels west at −4 m/s continuously. Determine their first actual encounter time and position. At that time calculate A's total distance and displacement; justify why a naïve first-stage root is invalid.
stages.reconstruct: First-stage model 4t=30−4t yields t=30/8=3.75 s, later than the 3 s reversal and so invalid. At t=3, A is at +12 m; for t≥3 its position is xA=12−(t−3)=15−t, while B has xB=30−4t. Set 15−t=30−4t gives t=5 s and x=10 m. A travelled 12 m east then 2 m west: distance=14 m, displacement=+10 m. Both final positions give x=10 and t≥3.
stages.diagnose: Does the first response apply the old xA=4t beyond t=3, forget continuity on reversal, or mistake net displacement for total distance?
stages.repair: Mark the reversal in a timeline, set xA from x(3)=12, solve the right-stage encounter and check path and displacement separately.
stages.boundary_test: If B's westward speed decreases to 1 m/s, test whether a meeting after reversal remains possible before calculating it.

core1b.fresh_task: A walker travels 24 m east in 6 s, rests 2 s, then walks 12 m west in 4 s. Choose the correct model to find overall average speed and signed average velocity. Explain why a single velocity magnitude is insufficient.

stages.predict: Predict whether signed average velocity may be smaller in magnitude than average speed on a journey with reversal.
stages.attempt: A walker travels 24 m east in 6 s, rests 2 s, then walks 12 m west in 4 s. Choose the correct model to find overall average speed and signed average velocity. Explain why a single velocity magnitude is insufficient.
stages.reconstruct: Total time=12 s; path length=24+12=36 m and net displacement=24−12=+12 m. Average speed=36/12=3 m/s and average velocity=+12/12=+1 m/s. Rest adds time but zero path and displacement.
stages.diagnose: Check whether the answer ignored rest, used path length in average velocity, or applied a sign incorrectly.
stages.repair: Create a two-column path/signed-displacement ledger, include rest in total duration, and recompute.
stages.boundary_test: If the walker walks 24 m west instead of 12 m, determine which average becomes zero and whether the average speed changes.

stages.predict: Predict the final position if a route's total distance is nonzero but east/west legs are equal.
stages.attempt: A school tracker lists successive displacement legs +9 m in 3 s, −4 m in 2 s, +7 m in 1 s. Draw a labelled x–t segment graph on a shared axis and give net displacement and total distance.
stages.reconstruct: Cumulative positions from origin are x=0 at t0, 9 at t3, 5 at t5 and 12 at t6. The x–t slopes are +3, −2, +7 m/s. Net displacement +12 m and path distance 9+4+7=20 m.
stages.diagnose: Distinguish copying leg displacements as absolute positions from a slip in summing the legs.
stages.repair: Start from x0 and update the cumulative position after every segment; verify slope and endpoint.
stages.boundary_test: If the original position is −5 m rather than 0, how do the plotted positions and signed slopes change?

core1b.fresh_task: A hiker travels east and then west over 25 seconds. Their total distance is 90 m and their final displacement is +18 m. Recover both leg lengths and calculate both interval averages. Check the reconstructed route.
core1b.protected_work: Recover two travel-leg lengths from total distance and net displacement, then compare average speed and velocity.

stages.predict: For a trip with total path length larger than its net displacement, predict whether some motion occurred in the opposite direction.
stages.attempt: A hiker travels east and then west over 25 seconds. Their total distance is 90 m and their final displacement is +18 m. Recover both leg lengths and calculate both interval averages. Check the reconstructed route.
stages.reconstruct: E+W=90; E−W=18; adding gives E=54 m, W=36 m. Average speed 90/25=3.6 m/s; average velocity +18/25=+0.72 m/s. Both leg lengths are nonnegative and satisfy the given sums.
stages.diagnose: Did the learner set both leg lengths positive in the displacement equation or confuse duration with distance?
stages.repair: Solve the distance and signed-displacement equations together and check both recovered givens.
stages.boundary_test: Keeping total distance 90 m but changing displacement to +100 m, explain why the revised givens are physically impossible.

core1b.fresh_task: A data logger records x=+7 m at t=0, x=+13 m at t=3 and x=+13 m at t=6. To determine motion at t=5 s, choose between (A) x–t graph height, (B) x–t slope, and (C) area under an x–t graph. Defend the model and find the velocity.
core1b.protected_work: Choose whether a position-time slope or velocity-time area can answer the question, and defend the chosen correspondence.

stages.predict: A position-time graph is flat while its vertical coordinate is +15 m. Predict the object's velocity.
stages.attempt: A data logger records x=+7 m at t=0, x=+13 m at t=3 and x=+13 m at t=6. To determine motion at t=5 s, choose between (A) x–t graph height, (B) x–t slope, and (C) area under an x–t graph. Defend the model and find the velocity.
stages.reconstruct: Choose slope of position–time: 0–3 s gives +2 m/s, 3–6 s gives zero. At t=5 the cart is stationary even though its position is +13 m. Height is position, and area of x–t is not displacement under this elementary model.
stages.diagnose: Check whether the learner mistook x–t height as speed, selected graph area without checking units, or performed the slope calculation incorrectly.
stages.repair: Label both axes and use Δx/Δt over the exact interval containing t=5.
stages.boundary_test: If every position is shifted by +20 m, does the velocity at t=5 change? Explain via slope.

core1b.fresh_task: An x–t log gives t=0,3,7,9 seconds with positions x=+6,+6,−2,+2 m. Reconstruct its three signed velocity steps; calculate the signed area sum and the total distance.
core1b.protected_work: Construct the correct signed velocity-time segments from a position-time table including a stationary interval and direction change.

stages.predict: Predict the sign of velocity when the x–t graph passes through the origin from positive to negative position.
stages.attempt: An x–t log gives t=0,3,7,9 seconds with positions x=+6,+6,−2,+2 m. Reconstruct its three signed velocity steps; calculate the signed area sum and the total distance.
stages.reconstruct: 0–3: zero velocity; 3–7: Δx=−8 over 4 s, velocity −2 m/s; 7–9: Δx=+4 over 2 s, velocity +2 m/s. Net Δx=−4 m, matching +2−(+6); total distance=0+8+4=12 m.
stages.diagnose: Find whether crossing zero was assumed to imply stopping, or the graph's slope was read with the wrong sign.
stages.repair: Calculate slope separately by consecutive position points, sketch signed v steps, then back-translate their areas.
stages.boundary_test: If the time labels are all doubled while positions remain unchanged, how do velocities and the displacement change?

core1b.fresh_task: An object has v=+3 m/s for 4 s, v=−2 m/s for 2 s, then an unknown constant velocity for 3 s. Its total displacement is +5 m. Find the final segment's signed velocity, full distance and final position if x0=−2 m.
core1b.protected_work: Determine a missing constant-velocity segment from a reported signed displacement, with a model-consistency check.

stages.predict: If the signed area below the time axis grows in magnitude, predict the effect on net displacement.
stages.attempt: An object has v=+3 m/s for 4 s, v=−2 m/s for 2 s, then an unknown constant velocity for 3 s. Its total displacement is +5 m. Find the final segment's signed velocity, full distance and final position if x0=−2 m.
stages.reconstruct: Known areas +12 and −4 give +8 m. The last stage must supply −3 m across 3 s, so v_last=−1 m/s. Total path distance=12+4+3=19 m; final x=−2+5=+3 m. Reverse-integrating signed areas confirms the endpoint.
stages.diagnose: Did the learner assign +1 instead of −1 to the missing velocity or confuse final position and displacement?
stages.repair: Set signed-area sum equal to the given displacement and solve the last segment; then separately sum absolute areas.
stages.boundary_test: If the target displacement were +14 m instead, would the final segment's direction reverse? Give the new sign.

core1b.fresh_task: A kayak moves east at 4 m/s relative to the water; the current carries the water west at 1 m/s relative to shore. Another craft starts 24 m behind the kayak and travels east at 5 m/s relative to shore. Determine the kayak's shore velocity and overtaking time, stating the frame for every number.
core1b.protected_work: Identify the frame and compose velocities correctly when a walker moves on a moving walkway; defend the chosen model.

stages.predict: Predict which motion looks eastbound to an observer moving west.
stages.attempt: A kayak moves east at 4 m/s relative to the water; the current carries the water west at 1 m/s relative to shore. Another craft starts 24 m behind the kayak and travels east at 5 m/s relative to shore. Determine the kayak's shore velocity and overtaking time, stating the frame for every number.
stages.reconstruct: Kayak velocity relative shore is +4−1=+3 m/s. The rear craft gains at +5−3=+2 m/s, so it covers the 24 m gap in 12 s. This is overtaking, not head-on motion; using 5+3 would confuse the directions.
stages.diagnose: Check whether frame labels or the signed closing rate were wrong; distinguish that from a division slip.
stages.repair: Compose water-relative and shore-relative velocities on one signed number line; use relative closing velocity.
stages.boundary_test: What if the rear craft moves at only +2 m/s relative to shore? Explain whether it can overtake.

core1b.fresh_task: An elevator's recorded vertical positions (up positive) are t=(0,3,6,8) s and y=(5,−1,−1,3) m. Construct a velocity-time diagram, calculate the net displacement and total distance, and explain the level section.
core1b.protected_work: Construct signed velocity-time representation from position-time data and distinguish the invariant displacement from distance.

stages.predict: Which segments have negative velocity when an object crosses the origin?
stages.attempt: An elevator's recorded vertical positions (up positive) are t=(0,3,6,8) s and y=(5,−1,−1,3) m. Construct a velocity-time diagram, calculate the net displacement and total distance, and explain the level section.
stages.reconstruct: From 0–3 s, Δy=−6 m and v=−2 m/s; 3–6 s is stationary v=0; 6–8 s, Δy=+4 m and v=+2 m/s. Net displacement is −2 m, equal to 3−5. Total distance is 6+4=10 m.
stages.diagnose: Was the initial height incorrectly assumed zero? Did the learner treat the stationary segment as reversal?
stages.repair: Use slope per interval, back-integrate the velocity steps, and compare against the original y values.
stages.boundary_test: Shift every recorded position upward by 10 m. Predict how the velocity graph and displacement change.

core1b.fresh_task: Cyclist A starts at x=0 and rides east at 4 m/s from t=0. Cyclist B is at x=30 m and remains at rest until t=2 s, then rides west at 3 m/s. At which global time do they meet? Verify both time intervals.
core1b.protected_work: Recognize that the first-stage meeting time is outside its interval and construct a valid post-reversal or post-delay encounter model.

stages.predict: Can delaying departure change which interval contains a meeting?
stages.attempt: Cyclist A starts at x=0 and rides east at 4 m/s from t=0. Cyclist B is at x=30 m and remains at rest until t=2 s, then rides west at 3 m/s. At which global time do they meet? Verify both time intervals.
stages.reconstruct: For 0≤t≤2, A is at x=4t≤8 and B remains at x=30, so no meeting. For t≥2, B has x=30−3(t−2)=36−3t. Equating 4t=36−3t gives t=36/7≈5.14 s, after the departure time. Meeting position is x=144/7≈20.57 m, matching B's expression.
stages.diagnose: Did the learner start B's clock at t=0 rather than t=2, or fail to distinguish waiting and moving stages?
stages.repair: Create a global clock, enforce continuity at t=2, and solve only within the correct segment.
stages.boundary_test: If B never departs, when does A reach x=30? Explain why this limit is not found by simply setting B's moving speed to zero while retaining the same start assumption.
